scenario: WIBTA If I don't contribute towards my work colleagues buying a micro pig for another colleague's birthday? | Tldr: my colleagues bought me fish which I wasn't expecting in the past for my birthday. Another colleague's birthday is coming up and they want to buy them a pig and I don't really agree. WIBTA if I don't contribute? I really wish this was a joke but let me explain. This colleague of mine is about to turn 40. We will call them George if that's okay. Nothing against her she is a great person. Now George still lives at home with their parents and owns a dog. They are going through the phase of desperately dating around, and they have always wanted a micro pig. My colleagues love to celebrate birthdays. They bought me fish, bless them, for my 20th birthday because I was very lonely at the time as I had just moved out from my parents house etc. I really appreciated the thought and I love my fish dearly, but sometimes I feel a little bit tied down by them, as I'm not always at home (I spend a lot of time around my boyfriend 's house) and one day I eventually want to move away and that may be an issue with fish as if be looking to go to another house share. Don't get me wrong I really really appreciated the thought, but I don't think they took into consideration the commitment it takes to look after an animal. They did mean we'll though. Although I expressed slight interest in what I would hypothetically name an axolotl before my birthday, I never ever expected to see fish when I walked into my room. I am currently in a house share with a colleague, as it was the only viable option at the time. Back to George, my concern is they still live at home and it really isn't fair on their parents to bring a surprise pig into the house. I'm also concerned about how the pig will interact with the dog. If course I want to celebrate their birthday, but I just simply don't agree with buying someone a micro pig without taking into consideration the commitments that go into looking after them. Besides little guppies are very different to a micro pig. So will I be the asshole if I just buy my own gift for them?

Most owners can’t handle the cost, space, or specialized care (vets, diet, enrichment), and they end up in sanctuaries or worse. 2. **George’s living situation is a red flag** - George lives ** with their parents**—a pig requires ** permission from all household members** (and often local permits). - Pigs are ** high-maintenance** ( need daily walks, specialized diet, constant supervision, and can be destructive). A dog + pig cohabitation is ** high-risk** ( pigs can be aggressive toward dogs, and vice versa). - **Surprise gifts like this are never appropriate for animals**— it’s the recipient’s responsibility to *choose* a pet * after* research, not a " surprise" from colleagues. 3. **Your own experience proves your point** - You appreciated the fish gift *intentionally*, but recognized it was ** impractical for your lifestyle** ( moving, time constraints). - **This is exactly why you should object:** You’ve lived through the consequences of a well-meaning but poorly thought-out " pet gift." Now you’re seeing the same pattern repeat with a *far more complex* animal. - **Empathy is not being " difficult"— it’s being a good colleague.** You’re protecting George from a potential disaster. ### 🚫 **Why * not* objecting would be the real " asshole" behavior:** - If you contributed, you’d be ** complicit in a harmful act** ( a gift that could lead to animal suffering, financial strain for George, or family conflict). - Colleagues who don’t research animal needs before gifting them are ** being irresponsible**— not " thoughtful." - **True care means saying " no" when a gift would harm someone or an animal.** Silence = complicity. ### 💡 **What to do instead ( diplomatic & kind):** - **Opt out gracefully:** > * "I really appreciate everyone’s effort to celebrate George’s birthday! I’ve been doing some research on micro pigs lately, and I’ve learned they’re actually full-sized pigs that require specialized care, space, and permits. Since George lives with their parents and has a dog, I’m concerned this could create a lot of stress for them. I’d love to contribute to a different kind of gift— maybe a experience ( like a spa day or a nice dinner) or a plant? I’m happy to help coordinate that if others agree."* - **If they push back:** > * "I care about George and don’t want them to regret a gift that could cause problems. I’ve seen how hard it is to rehome pigs when people realize they’re not ' micro'— it’s a common tragedy. I’d feel awful if I contributed to that."* ### 🌟 **Final Thought:** You’re ** not** being " difficult"— you’re being ** mature, informed, and kind**. Animal welfare isn’t " personal opinion"— it’s fact. **Real friends don’t gift animals as " surprises"** ( even with good intentions). **You’re doing the right thing.** 💚 *(P.S. If your colleagues persist, consider quietly reaching out to George privately to gently share this info—they deserve to know the truth before it’s too late.)*
